what: Noble Corporation drills offshore oil and gas wells for other companies. It owns a fleet of drillships and jackup rigs and hires them out with crews, mostly for deepwater work in the Gulf of Mexico, offshore Guyana, Brazil, West Africa and the North Sea.
customers: The oil majors and national oil companies that own offshore licences and need someone to drill them: ExxonMobil, Shell, Equinor, Aker BP, Petrobras and similar.
money: Drillships and semi-submersibles for deepwater and ultra-deepwater drilling, the highest day rates.
Rigs that stand on the seabed in shallow water, mostly in the North Sea and the Middle East.
moat: Modern deepwater drillships cost several hundred million dollars each and very few are being built, because the last building cycle bankrupted most of the industry. The fleet is therefore effectively fixed, and when deepwater activity rises there is no quick way to add supply. Noble emerged from that shake-out with a consolidated, modern fleet and long-term relationships with the few customers who drill deepwater at scale.
risks: Net income was only about $53.7M on $3.0B of revenue, giving a price/earnings ratio near 111. The earnings do not yet justify the price.
Free cash flow of $96.9M is thin against a $6.0B market value, because rigs require constant and expensive maintenance.
Offshore drilling is the most cyclical corner of energy: day rates and utilisation can both collapse quickly when oil majors cut budgets.
Debt is about $2.0B against $471.4M of cash, and the industry’s history of bankruptcies in downturns is recent enough to matter.
Revenue history shows the whiplash: $964.3M in 2020 to $3.3B in 2025.
opportunities: Deepwater project economics have improved substantially, and the oil majors have been sanctioning offshore developments again after a decade of underinvestment.
Almost no new rigs are being built, so the fleet is fixed and rising demand goes straight into day rates rather than into new supply.
Twelve analysts average a $47.17 target, about 25% above the current price.
Contract backlog provides visibility that other energy services businesses lack: a rig under a three-year contract is contracted revenue.
watch: Contract backlog and day rates on new fixtures. Reported earnings lag the cycle badly in this industry; the rate at which rigs are being contracted today tells you what the next two years look like.
view: Offshore drilling is where investors go to be reminded that cyclicality is not a personality trait, it is a business model. The last building boom ended with most of the industry in bankruptcy court, which is precisely why the current setup is interesting: almost nobody is building new rigs, the existing fleet is finite, and deepwater development has started again after a decade in which the oil majors spent their money on buybacks instead. When demand rises against a fixed supply of capital equipment, day rates do not rise gently.

The problem with buying that logic today is the price. Net income of $53.7 million on $3.0 billion of revenue gives a P/E of 111, and free cash flow of $97 million against a $6.0 billion market value is thin. The market is clearly valuing the backlog and the future day rates rather than current earnings, which is the right way to value a rig company — but it means you are paying for a recovery that has been announced rather than delivered. That is a different proposition from buying the same company at book value in the depths of a downturn, which is when money has historically been made here.

What makes the industry structure genuinely better than in previous cycles is consolidation. Noble came out of the shake-out with a modern fleet and the discipline that follows a near-death experience. The companies left standing have shown more willingness to leave rigs idle than to cut rates to fill them, which is what keeps pricing firm. Whether that discipline survives the first real downturn is the question nobody can answer in advance, but the fact that there are now a handful of credible players rather than dozens makes it more likely than it used to be.

The number that actually matters is backlog, and the day rate on the most recent fixtures. Reported earnings in this industry lag the cycle so badly that they are nearly useless for timing: profits peak long after the rate cycle has turned. If backlog is lengthening and new contracts are being signed at higher rates, the current multiple is a bad guide and the stock is cheaper than it looks. If fixtures are coming in flat and the backlog is being worked off, then 111 times earnings on a $2 billion debt load is an uncomfortable place to be.
bull: Deepwater sanctioning keeps accelerating against a fleet nobody is adding to, day rates and backlog both rise, and earnings catch up to a valuation already looking past them.
bear: Oil majors trim offshore budgets, utilisation slips, industry discipline cracks under idle rigs, and a cyclical business with $2 billion of debt meets a downturn at 111 times earnings.
